extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examiners on identifying and analyzing judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, mental processes, laws/natural phenomena, products of nature) under 35 U.S.C. § 101, including when and how to apply the markedly different characteristics analysis and the tentative abstract idea procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims requiring a computer may still recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims can recite a mental process even if they are claimed as being performed on a computer (e.g., Benson; Mortgage Grader).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating whether a claim that requires a computer recites a mental process, examiners should carefully consider the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim in light of the specification. Review the specification to determine if the claimed invention is described as a concept that is performed in the human mind and applicant is merely claiming that concept performed (1) on a generic computer, (2) in a computer environment, or (3) merely using a computer as a tool. In those situations the claim is considered to recite a mental process. Case citations: Benson (algorithm could be performed mentally), Mortgage Grader (anonymous loan shopping could be performed by humans).

rubrics_metrics.name: Performing a mental process on a generic computer
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed mental process performed on a generic computer may be an abstract idea (example: Voter Verified; Versata).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification describes steps as human cognitive actions historically performed by people, the fact that the steps are performed on generic computer hardware does not necessarily make the claim non-abstract. Examples: Voter Verified (voting/verification steps are "human cognitive actions"); Versata (determining a price implemented using general purpose computer hardware was still directed to abstract idea). Use specification and case law to determine whether the computer adds anything other than generic implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performing a mental process in a computer environment
rubrics_metrics.description: A mental process performed in a computer environment (i.e., describing how systems receive, screen, distribute data analogous to human action) can be directed to an abstract idea (example: Symantec; FairWarning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should evaluate whether the claimed computer-environment steps merely mirror human decision-making (e.g., screening mail or detecting misuse) and lack claim limitations that foreclose performance by a human. If the claims, aside from generic computer-implemented steps, can be performed mentally or with pen and paper, treat as an abstract idea. Use specification support and relevant Federal Circuit decisions to support the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using a computer as a tool to perform a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely use a computer as a tool to perform processes humans can do mentally are directed to mental-process abstract ideas (examples: Mortgage Grader; Berkheimer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where claimed steps are recited at a high level of generality and the computer is just a tool for performing parsing, comparing, grading, or other cognitive activities, the claim is likely directed to a mental process. Cite cases where the concept itself (e.g., anonymous loan shopping; parsing/comparing data) is identified as the abstract idea despite computer implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Both product and process claims may recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: Product claims (e.g., systems, computer-readable media) and process claims alike may recite mental processes and thus be directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume only method claims recite mental processes. Examples of product claims reciting mental processes include content extraction APIs, anonymous loan shopping systems, computer-readable media with fraud-detection instructions, electronic post offices, self-verifying voting systems, monitoring systems, and storage media implementing pricing methods (cases cited: Content Extraction; Mortgage Grader; CyberSource; Symantec; Voter Verified; Electric Power Group; Versata). For such claims, analyze whether the claimed product merely embodies a mental-process concept implemented generically by hardware or code. Treat the phrase "mental processes" as referring to the type of abstract idea, not the statutory claim category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tentative abstract idea procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: If an examiner believes a claim limitation should be treated as an abstract idea but it does not fall within the enumerated groupings, treat it as a "tentative abstract idea" and follow the prescribed procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the subject matter eligibility framework: (a) If the claim as a whole integrates the tentative abstract idea into a practical application → Step 2A: NO (eligible at Pathway B). (b) If not integrated → Step 2A: YES (directed to a judicial exception) → proceed to Step 2B: if the claim as a whole provides an inventive concept → eligible at Pathway C; if not → examiner should bring the application to the attention of the Technology Center (TC) director. A rejection of a claim reciting a tentative abstract idea must be approved by the TC director (approval indicated in the file) and justified in the record. The TC Director's approval triggers use of form paragraph 7.05.017 and the TC Director's signature; Patents Management will notify the public (e.g., USPTO website). Examiners may conduct interviews in response to Step 2B rejections; TC Director interview is not necessary for the examiner to withdraw/maintain the rejection. Examiners are not required to obtain TC Director approval to withdraw or maintain such a §101 rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of nature and natural phenomena exceptions (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles/relations and nature-based products that are naturally occurring or do not have markedly different characteristics compared to what occurs in nature; these are judicial exceptions to patent eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The basic tools of science and technology are not patentable (cases: Funk Bros.; Diamond v. Chakrabarty). Examples courts have identified as laws/natural phenomena include isolated DNA (Myriad), cloned animals (Roslin), correlations involving DNA, metabolic correlations (Mayo), correlations between biomarkers and disease risk (Cleveland Clinic v. True Health), electromagnetism (O’Reilly v. Morse), bacterial qualities (Funk), primers (Ambry), chemical principles (Tilghman), cell-free fetal DNA (Ariosa), genotype–drug response correlations (Vanda). However, not every claim that describes a natural ability or product is an exception; claims that apply or transform natural phenomena (e.g., treatment methods, manufacturing processes) may be eligible (examples: Rapid Litigation Mgmt. v. CellzDirect; Tilghman). If a claim recites a law/natural phenomenon, further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two is needed to determine whether the claim integrates the exception into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Products of nature (definition and scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a law of nature or natural phenomenon is claimed as a physical product it may be treated as a "product of nature"; this includes naturally occurring products and non‑naturally occurring products that lack markedly different characteristics from their natural counterparts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: isolated DNA (Myriad), cloned animals (Roslin), bacterial mixtures (Funk). The Office treats "law of nature," "natural phenomenon," and "product of nature" inclusively for Step 2A analysis. Non-naturally occurring products that are structurally identical to natural counterparts remain products of nature (Ambry). The key inquiry for non-naturally occurring products is whether they possess "markedly different characteristics" from natural counterparts. If a claim recites a nature-based product limitation, apply the markedly different characteristics analysis (MPEP §2106.04(c)) to determine whether the limitation is a product-of-nature exception. If the claim clearly does not tie up a judicial exception, consider the streamlined analysis in §2106.06.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis — when to perform
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the markedly different characteristics analysis only to the nature-based product limitations in a claim to determine whether those products are "product of nature" exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful not to overextend the analysis to claim elements that are not nature-based when the claim as a whole is not nature-based. If the nature-based product limitation is naturally occurring, no need to perform the analysis because it is by definition directed to a naturally occurring product and falls under the product of nature exception. For claims that include nature-based products as only part of a larger claimed invention, analyze whether the claim also recites another exception that would require further eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis — how to perform and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the claimed nature-based product to its naturally occurring counterpart to determine whether it possesses markedly different characteristics; this analysis informs Step 2A Prong One.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed nature-based product has markedly different characteristics, the claim does not recite a product-of-nature exception and is eligible at Step 2A: NO (Pathway B), unless another exception applies. For claims where the entire claim is a single nature-based product, showing a markedly different characteristic in that product obviates further analysis (no Step 2B needed). If the nature-based product does not exhibit markedly different characteristics from a naturally occurring counterpart, the claim recites a product-of-nature exception and requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two (and possibly Step 2B). Use Chakrabarty and Roslin comparisons as precedents (compare claimed bacterium/sheep to naturally occurring counterparts).

rubrics_metrics.name: BRI and claim-drafting recommendations for nature-based products
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of claims, a nature-based product limitation may encompass both eligible and ineligible embodiments; examiners should address this in prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim's BRI encompasses both markedly different and not markedly different embodiments (e.g., "cloned giraffe" might cover both types), then the claim may recite a product of nature and requires further analysis. If a claim is ultimately rejected for failing to encompass an inventive concept (Step 2B: NO), it is best practice for the examiner to point out the BRI in the Office action and recommend an amendment to narrow the claim to embodiments that are not directed to products of nature or otherwise eligible. For claims that recite a nature-based product limitation but clearly do not tie up any judicial exception, consider the streamlined eligibility analysis in MPEP §2106.06.
